newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Market slump seen far from over.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Market slump seen far from over.

text.p: After getting slammed by a slew of stronger-than-expected economic data on the first day of active trading in 1997, U.S. credit markets may get some help from friendlier second-tier data on Friday, analysts said.
But they cautioned that if anything is going to help Treasuries escape from their current doldrums in the near term, it will likely be technicals rather than fundamentals.
The 1000 EST/1500 GMT report on November construction spending may provide fodder for some price movements, although the number rarely draws much attention, experts said.
Cary Leahy, senior economist at Lehman Brothers Inc, said construction spending may be a glimmer of hope because it should show a decline in November, following three months of gains.
On average, economists in a Reuters poll forecast the report would show construction spending fell 0.4 percent in November after a 1.8 percent rise in October.

"But you will get more reaction to a bad number than a good number," Leahy said. "If you get a decline, the market may ignore it. If you get an increase, the market may selloff a little bit more," he added.
After ending 1996 with a sour session on Tuesday, Treasuries began 1997 by falling again on Thursday after a string of data showed signs of a stronger economy.

Notably, the National Association of Purchasing Managers Index reported the highest reading since June, 1996 of its index of manufacturing activity. The index rose to 54.0 in December, exceeding market forecasts for a 51.5 reading, and up from 52.7 in the previous month.
Experts said bond markets were also spooked on Thursday by a three-point increase in the Conference Board's help-wanted index to 85.0 in November, and a sharp drop in stock prices.
Some market analysts said a shift in the current negative sentiment may be a difficult task, even if construction spending figures are weak.

"I don't think you are going to see a sudden shift in sentiment or psychology tomorrow, especially without any major numbers being released," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
He said the market will have to wait for top-tier data next week, such as payrolls next Friday.
Apart from construction spending numbers, analysts said technical factors might help Treasuries rebound in the Friday session where significant new data will be scarce.
Terence Gabriel, technical analyst at I.D.E.A., suggested that even though the March bond contract broke thorugh two-week lows Thursday, the bond should find support in the low 111 range.
"From there, I think the market can rally back up, but I think it is going to have a very hard time," he said.
